aws_access_analyzer_analyzer: `aws_access_analyzer_analyzer` creates an IAM Access Analyzer, a real analyzer that continuously scans resource policies (S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, and similar) and reports which grant access to anything outside the account or organization it's scoped to. Analyzers come in a few real, distinct modes, external access, unused access, and internal access, and the same resource also drives policy validation and policy generation from real CloudTrail activity.
aws_account_access_application: `aws_account_access_application` is part of IAM Identity Center's account access manager, which manages applications and entitlements that grant Identity Center principals access to IAM roles across accounts. An application in this context represents one such cross-account access grant, connecting a principal to a real IAM role in a target account without a standalone permission set.
aws_account_access_entitlement: `aws_account_access_entitlement` is the entitlement half of IAM Identity Center's account access manager, the specific permission grant attached to an `aws_account_access_application`. It is what actually authorizes a principal to assume the application's target role, real, revocable access rather than an implicit side effect of the application existing.
aws_acmpca_certificate: `aws_acmpca_certificate` is a certificate issued by an `aws_acmpca_certificate_authority`. AWS Private CA issues it against the CA's own signing key and policy, the certificate itself carries no independent configuration beyond what its issuing CA allows.
aws_acmpca_certificate_authority: `aws_acmpca_certificate_authority` creates a private certificate authority, root or subordinate, that issues and revokes X.509 certificates for internal PKI. It's regionally scoped, integrates with services like ACM and IoT Core for automated certificate issuance, and its private key never leaves AWS's managed HSM boundary.
aws_agent_registry_registry: `aws_agent_registry_registry` creates a private, governed catalog for discovering agents, tools, skills, and MCP servers inside Bedrock AgentCore. It's the container that org-wide publishing and discovery of these resources happens through, rather than each team maintaining its own ad hoc list.
aws_agent_registry_registry_record: `aws_agent_registry_registry_record` represents the metadata for one individual resource, an agent, a tool, an MCP server, published into an `aws_agent_registry_registry`. It's the actual catalog entry a consumer discovers and resolves, not the underlying resource itself.
aws_aiops_investigation_group: `aws_aiops_investigation_group` is a one-time setup resource for CloudWatch investigations, the generative AI-assisted incident response capability that correlates signals across an account during an active issue. One investigation group per region holds the central settings, encryption and retention among them, that every investigation in that region inherits.
aws_amazon_mq_broker: `aws_amazon_mq_broker` creates the actual message broker environment, ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ, that Amazon MQ runs. It's the basic building block of the service, everything else, configuration, users, network placement, attaches to a broker rather than existing independently.
aws_amazon_mq_configuration: `aws_amazon_mq_configuration` defines the engine-specific settings (XML for ActiveMQ, a config file for RabbitMQ) that an `aws_amazon_mq_broker` runs with, kept as a separate, versioned resource so the same configuration can be validated and reused across brokers instead of being edited in place on each one.
aws_amazon_mq_configuration_association: `aws_amazon_mq_configuration_association` is the real link between an `aws_amazon_mq_configuration` and the `aws_amazon_mq_broker` it applies to. A configuration on its own changes nothing, this association is what actually applies a given configuration revision to a running broker.
aws_amplify_app: `aws_amplify_app` creates the top-level Amplify Hosting application, the Git-connected project that Amplify's managed CI/CD pipeline builds and deploys from. Branches, domains, and build settings all attach to this app rather than standing alone.
aws_amplify_branch: `aws_amplify_branch` connects one Git branch of an `aws_amplify_app` to its own real, independently deployed environment, so pushing to `main` and pushing to a feature branch produce two separate, live URLs rather than one shared deployment.
aws_amplify_domain: `aws_amplify_domain` attaches a custom domain to an `aws_amplify_app` and maps its subdomains to specific branches, real DNS and SSL provisioning included, rather than leaving the app reachable only at its default `amplifyapp.com` URL.
aws_amplify_uibuilder_component: `aws_amplify_uibuilder_component` is a UI component generated by Amplify Studio, commonly converted automatically from a Figma design into real, editable React component code rather than hand-written from scratch.
aws_amplify_uibuilder_form: `aws_amplify_uibuilder_form` is Amplify Studio's form-building counterpart to `aws_amplify_uibuilder_component`, a generated, data-bound form definition rather than a hand-assembled one, wired to an app's real data model.
aws_amplify_uibuilder_theme: `aws_amplify_uibuilder_theme` defines the shared visual styling, colors, typography, spacing, that Amplify Studio applies consistently across an app's generated components and forms, so design changes happen in one place rather than per component.
aws_api_gateway_account: `aws_api_gateway_account` configures account-wide REST API Gateway settings, most notably the IAM role API Gateway assumes to push execution logs to CloudWatch, applying once per account rather than per `aws_api_gateway_rest_api`.
aws_api_gateway_api_key: `aws_api_gateway_api_key` issues a key that identifies a caller against an `aws_api_gateway_usage_plan`, the real mechanism REST APIs use to meter and throttle usage per consumer rather than per IAM identity.
aws_api_gateway_authorizer: `aws_api_gateway_authorizer` attaches a Lambda-, Cognito-, or IAM-based access-control check to an `aws_api_gateway_rest_api`, run before a request reaches its backend integration, so authorization logic lives outside the backend rather than duplicated inside it.
aws_api_gateway_base_path_mapping: `aws_api_gateway_base_path_mapping` maps a path segment on an `aws_api_gateway_domain_name` to a specific REST API and stage, the real mechanism that lets one custom domain front several different APIs at different base paths.
aws_api_gateway_client_certificate: `aws_api_gateway_client_certificate` generates a certificate an `aws_api_gateway_rest_api` presents to its own backend, so the backend can verify requests genuinely came through API Gateway rather than directly from the internet.
aws_api_gateway_deployment: `aws_api_gateway_deployment` is a real, immutable snapshot of an `aws_api_gateway_rest_api`'s resources and methods at a point in time. A REST API's configuration only takes effect once deployed, and a deployment only becomes reachable once an `aws_api_gateway_stage` points to it.
aws_api_gateway_documentation_part: `aws_api_gateway_documentation_part` is one documented fragment, a description of a specific method, resource, or parameter, that rolls up into an `aws_api_gateway_documentation_version` for an `aws_api_gateway_rest_api`.
aws_api_gateway_documentation_version: `aws_api_gateway_documentation_version` snapshots an `aws_api_gateway_rest_api`'s documentation parts at a point in time, kept versioned separately from the API's own deployments so docs and API behavior can each move independently.
aws_api_gateway_domain_name: `aws_api_gateway_domain_name` registers a custom domain for REST APIs (API Gateway v1), provisioning the TLS certificate and edge or regional endpoint that requests to that domain terminate at, before `aws_api_gateway_base_path_mapping` routes them to a specific API.
aws_api_gateway_domain_name_v2: `aws_api_gateway_domain_name_v2` is the newer resource type for the same custom-domain concept as `aws_api_gateway_domain_name`, supporting multi-level base path mappings that the original resource type doesn't.
aws_api_gateway_gateway_response: `aws_api_gateway_gateway_response` customizes the response API Gateway itself returns for a given error, a 4XX or 5XX that never reached the backend, on an `aws_api_gateway_rest_api`, overriding the default generic error body and headers.
aws_api_gateway_method: `aws_api_gateway_method` defines one HTTP method (GET, POST, and similar) on an `aws_api_gateway_resource`, together with its own authorization, request validation, and backend integration, the real unit a REST API caller actually invokes.
aws_api_gateway_model: `aws_api_gateway_model` is a JSON Schema definition attached to an `aws_api_gateway_rest_api`, used by request validators and documentation to describe the real shape of a request or response body rather than leaving it untyped.
aws_api_gateway_request_validator: `aws_api_gateway_request_validator` attaches to an `aws_api_gateway_method` and rejects malformed requests, missing required parameters or a body that doesn't match its `aws_api_gateway_model`, before they ever reach the backend integration.
aws_api_gateway_resource: `aws_api_gateway_resource` defines one path segment in a REST API's URL tree, nested under an `aws_api_gateway_rest_api` (or under another resource), with one or more `aws_api_gateway_method`s attached to actually handle requests at that path.
aws_api_gateway_rest_api: `aws_api_gateway_rest_api` creates the REST API itself, the container for an API Gateway v1 (REST API) deployment. Resources, methods, and deployments all nest inside it, and it's the unit that gets versioned and deployed to a stage as a whole.
aws_api_gateway_stage: `aws_api_gateway_stage` is a named, addressable environment (`prod`, `dev`, and similar) that points at a specific `aws_api_gateway_deployment`. Callers hit a stage's own URL, and promoting a new version means moving the stage to point at a new deployment, not editing the API in place.
aws_api_gateway_usage_plan: `aws_api_gateway_usage_plan` defines throttling and quota limits for one or more REST APIs and stages, and the `aws_api_gateway_api_key`s associated with it are what identify which caller a given request's usage counts against.
aws_api_gateway_usage_plan_key: `aws_api_gateway_usage_plan_key` is the actual association between an `aws_api_gateway_api_key` and an `aws_api_gateway_usage_plan`. An API key on its own is subject to no limits, this association is what puts it under a specific plan's throttling and quota.
aws_api_gateway_v2_api: `aws_api_gateway_v2_api` creates an HTTP API or WebSocket API, API Gateway v2's lighter-weight, lower-latency alternative to a v1 REST API, purpose-built for proxying to Lambda or an HTTP backend rather than the full feature set REST APIs offer.
aws_api_gateway_v2_api_gateway_managed_o: `aws_api_gateway_v2_api_gateway_managed_overrides` lets specific settings on an API Gateway-managed `aws_api_gateway_v2_stage` be overridden without disconnecting the stage from Gateway's own automatic management of it.
aws_api_gateway_v2_api_mapping: `aws_api_gateway_v2_api_mapping` maps an `aws_api_gateway_v2_api` and stage onto a path under an `aws_api_gateway_v2_domain_name`, the v2 equivalent of a v1 base path mapping.
aws_api_gateway_v2_authorizer: `aws_api_gateway_v2_authorizer` attaches a Lambda-, JWT-, or IAM-based access check to an `aws_api_gateway_v2_api`, evaluated before a request reaches its integration, the v2 counterpart to a v1 REST API authorizer.
aws_api_gateway_v2_deployment: `aws_api_gateway_v2_deployment` is a snapshot of an `aws_api_gateway_v2_api`'s routes and integrations at a point in time, the v2 counterpart to a v1 REST API deployment, made reachable once an `aws_api_gateway_v2_stage` points to it.
aws_api_gateway_v2_domain_name: `aws_api_gateway_v2_domain_name` registers a custom domain for HTTP or WebSocket APIs, provisioning the TLS certificate and endpoint that requests terminate at before an `aws_api_gateway_v2_api_mapping` routes them to a specific API and stage.
aws_api_gateway_v2_integration: `aws_api_gateway_v2_integration` connects an `aws_api_gateway_v2_api`'s routes to a real backend, Lambda, an HTTP endpoint, or another AWS service, the actual mechanism that determines what happens once a request matches a route.
aws_api_gateway_v2_integration_response: `aws_api_gateway_v2_integration_response` transforms the response an `aws_api_gateway_v2_integration` returns before it goes back to the caller, used on WebSocket APIs where response mapping isn't handled automatically the way it is for HTTP APIs.
aws_api_gateway_v2_model: `aws_api_gateway_v2_model` is a JSON Schema definition attached to an `aws_api_gateway_v2_api`, the v2 counterpart to a v1 REST API model, describing the expected shape of a request or response body.
aws_api_gateway_v2_route_response: `aws_api_gateway_v2_route_response` defines the response a WebSocket API route sends back after its `aws_api_gateway_v2_integration_response` runs, part of the two-way message flow WebSocket APIs support that HTTP APIs don't need.
aws_api_gateway_v2_routing_rule: `aws_api_gateway_v2_routing_rule` defines additional request-matching logic for an `aws_api_gateway_v2_api`'s routes beyond the basic method-and-path match, used to route the same path differently based on request content.
aws_api_gateway_v2_stage: `aws_api_gateway_v2_stage` is a named, addressable environment for an HTTP or WebSocket API that points at a specific `aws_api_gateway_v2_deployment`, the v2 counterpart to a v1 REST API stage.
aws_api_gateway_v2_vpc_link: `aws_api_gateway_v2_vpc_link` lets an `aws_api_gateway_v2_api` integration reach a private resource inside a VPC (an internal load balancer, for instance) without that resource being exposed to the public internet, the v2 counterpart to a v1 REST API VPC link.
aws_api_gateway_vpc_link: `aws_api_gateway_vpc_link` lets a REST API's integration reach a private resource inside a VPC, typically a Network Load Balancer in front of an internal service, without that resource ever being exposed publicly.
aws_app_config_application: `aws_app_config_application` is the top-level container in AWS AppConfig, the logical grouping that an `aws_app_config_environment` and `aws_app_config_configuration_profile` both attach to. AppConfig itself lets you change application behavior, feature flags, allow lists, throttling limits, in production without redeploying code.
aws_app_config_configuration_profile: `aws_app_config_configuration_profile` defines how AppConfig locates and manages one piece of configuration data, either a feature-flag profile or a free-form configuration sourced from S3, SSM Parameter Store, Secrets Manager, or AppConfig's own hosted store, with optional validators that block a bad deployment before it ships.
aws_app_config_deployment: `aws_app_config_deployment` starts the actual rollout of a specific configuration version to an `aws_app_config_environment`, following a chosen `aws_app_config_deployment_strategy` and validated against any validators the `aws_app_config_configuration_profile` defines, with automatic CloudWatch-alarm-triggered rollback if something breaks mid-rollout.
aws_app_config_deployment_strategy: `aws_app_config_deployment_strategy` defines how gradually a configuration change rolls out, the percentage growth rate and bake time between steps, so a change reaches a small slice of an environment first and only expands once it's proven safe.
aws_app_config_environment: `aws_app_config_environment` is a logical deployment target inside an `aws_app_config_application`, Beta or Production for the whole app, or Web, Mobile, and Backend for its subcomponents, with its own CloudWatch alarms that AppConfig monitors during a deployment and rolls back on if one trips.
aws_app_config_experiment_definition: `aws_app_config_experiment_definition` runs a real A/B test or gradual rollout on production traffic, built directly on top of AppConfig's own feature-flag configuration profiles rather than a separate experimentation stack, splitting traffic between variants and tracking operational metrics through CloudWatch as exposure increases.
aws_app_config_extension: `aws_app_config_extension` defines custom or AWS-authored behavior, notify SNS or EventBridge, run a Lambda check, that AppConfig invokes at specific lifecycle points (before a hosted configuration is created, or when a deployment starts, completes, or rolls back).
aws_app_config_extension_association: `aws_app_config_extension_association` attaches an `aws_app_config_extension` to a specific AppConfig resource, an application or a configuration profile, and is what actually invokes the extension at its defined lifecycle points. An extension defined but never associated never runs.
aws_app_flow_connector_profile: `aws_app_flow_connector_profile` stores the authenticated connection details, credentials and endpoint, for one SaaS source or destination (Salesforce, Zendesk, Slack, and similar), that an `aws_app_flow_flow` then draws on to move data without re-authenticating per flow.
aws_app_flow_flow: `aws_app_flow_flow` defines one real data transfer between a source and destination, on demand or on a schedule, using the connections an `aws_app_flow_connector_profile` establishes. It's the actual unit of work Amazon AppFlow runs, field mappings, transformations, and trigger included.
aws_app_integrations_application: `aws_app_integrations_application` configures a reusable connection to an external application inside Amazon AppIntegrations, most commonly consumed by Amazon Connect's own third-party integrations, the general application-level counterpart to a specific `aws_app_integrations_data_integration` or `aws_app_integrations_event_integration`.
aws_app_integrations_data_integration: `aws_app_integrations_data_integration` configures a bulk or bidirectional data connection to an external application, defining what data AppIntegrations pulls in and how it's kept current, distinct from the real-time streaming an `aws_app_integrations_event_integration` handles.
aws_app_integrations_event_integration: `aws_app_integrations_event_integration` streams events from a partner application into an EventBridge event bus, with its own filters and event sources, so downstream AWS services can react to changes in an external system in near real time rather than polling for them.
aws_app_mesh_gateway_route: `aws_app_mesh_gateway_route` matches incoming traffic at an `aws_app_mesh_virtual_gateway` and directs it to a virtual service inside the mesh, the ingress counterpart to the routes an `aws_app_mesh_virtual_router` uses for traffic already inside the mesh.
aws_app_mesh_mesh: `aws_app_mesh_mesh` creates the service mesh itself, the logical boundary for all network traffic between the services registered inside it. Every other App Mesh resource, virtual nodes, routers, services, gateways, belongs to exactly one mesh.
aws_app_mesh_virtual_gateway: `aws_app_mesh_virtual_gateway` is the entry point for traffic coming into an `aws_app_mesh_mesh` from outside it, running the same Envoy proxy technology as a virtual node but for ingress rather than for a specific service.
aws_app_mesh_virtual_node: `aws_app_mesh_virtual_node` is a logical pointer to one real, discoverable service (an ECS service, a Kubernetes deployment) inside an `aws_app_mesh_mesh`. The proxy deployed alongside that real service reads its virtual node's configuration to decide how to route outbound traffic.
aws_app_mesh_virtual_router: `aws_app_mesh_virtual_router` handles traffic for one or more `aws_app_mesh_virtual_service`s, with routes that distribute traffic across `aws_app_mesh_virtual_node`s by weighted percentage, HTTP header, path, or gRPC method, the mechanism behind canary and blue/green traffic shifts without touching application code.
aws_app_mesh_virtual_service: `aws_app_mesh_virtual_service` is an abstraction of a real service, backed either directly by an `aws_app_mesh_virtual_node` or indirectly through an `aws_app_mesh_virtual_router`, named to match the real service's own discoverable name so other services can keep addressing it exactly as they did before App Mesh was introduced.
aws_app_runner_auto_scaling_configuratio: `aws_app_runner_auto_scaling_configuration` sets the minimum and maximum provisioned instance count and per-instance concurrency an `aws_app_runner_service` scales within, letting a service scale down to its floor when traffic is low rather than running fixed capacity.
aws_app_runner_observability_configurati: `aws_app_runner_observability_configuration` enables AWS X-Ray tracing for an `aws_app_runner_service`, kept as its own resource so the same tracing configuration can be reused across multiple services rather than redefined on each one.
aws_app_runner_service: `aws_app_runner_service` deploys source code or a container image directly to a running, scalable, load-balanced web service, without the caller provisioning or choosing underlying compute, App Runner builds and operates it end to end.
aws_app_runner_vpc_connector: `aws_app_runner_vpc_connector` gives an `aws_app_runner_service` outbound access into a VPC, specifying the subnets and security groups it uses, so the service can reach a private database or internal API that isn't exposed to the public internet.
aws_app_runner_vpc_ingress_connection: `aws_app_runner_vpc_ingress_connection` restricts an `aws_app_runner_service` to only be reachable from inside a VPC, connecting the service to a VPC interface endpoint so it accepts no traffic from the public internet at all. A service can have at most one of these.
aws_app_stream_app_block: `aws_app_stream_app_block` packages the application files and setup script needed to stream one application, built by an `aws_app_stream_app_block_builder` and uploaded to S3, the app-block model that lets an application be added to a stack without baking it into a full image.
aws_app_stream_app_block_builder: `aws_app_stream_app_block_builder` is the virtual machine used to create an `aws_app_stream_app_block`, packaging installed application content and uploading it to S3 to complete the app block, the app-block equivalent of what an `aws_app_stream_image_builder` does for full images.
aws_app_stream_application: `aws_app_stream_application` contains the information needed to actually launch one application to a streaming user, referencing the `aws_app_stream_app_block` or image that holds its real files.
aws_app_stream_application_entitlement_a: `aws_app_stream_application_entitlement_association` links a specific `aws_app_stream_application` to an `aws_app_stream_entitlement`, the actual grant that makes that one application, rather than every application in the stack, subject to that entitlement's SAML-based access rule.
aws_app_stream_application_fleet_associa: `aws_app_stream_application_fleet_association` links an `aws_app_stream_application` to the `aws_app_stream_fleet` it's actually streamed from, real for the app-block model where an application isn't already baked into a fleet's own image.
aws_app_stream_directory_config: `aws_app_stream_directory_config` stores the details AppStream needs to join image builders and fleet instances to an Active Directory domain, in a specific organizational unit, so streamed sessions can authenticate against a real corporate directory.
aws_app_stream_entitlement: `aws_app_stream_entitlement` controls access to specific applications in an AppStream stack based on SAML assertions from the identity provider, letting access to individual applications, not just to a stack as a whole, be driven by real group membership or attributes asserted at sign-in.
aws_app_stream_fleet: `aws_app_stream_fleet` provisions the streaming instances, EC2 instances made available one-per-user for the duration of a session, that run the applications and desktops an `aws_app_stream_stack` streams. The instance is terminated automatically once the session ends.
aws_app_stream_image_builder: `aws_app_stream_image_builder` is a virtual machine used to install, configure, and test applications before capturing them into an immutable image. Once an image is created it can't be edited in place, changing it means building a new image from a fresh image builder.
aws_app_stream_stack: `aws_app_stream_stack` bundles an `aws_app_stream_fleet`, user access policies, and storage configuration into the unit that actually streams applications to users. Users are entitled to stacks, not directly to fleets.
aws_app_stream_stack_fleet_association: `aws_app_stream_stack_fleet_association` links an `aws_app_stream_stack` to the `aws_app_stream_fleet` that actually runs its streaming instances. A stack with no fleet association has user access policies and storage configured but nothing to stream from.
aws_app_sync_api: `aws_app_sync_api` creates a GraphQL API in AWS AppSync, a managed, serverless endpoint that resolves queries against one or more real backend data sources, with built-in subscriptions for pushing real-time updates to connected clients.
aws_app_sync_api_cache: `aws_app_sync_api_cache` enables server-side caching for an `aws_app_sync_api`, holding resolver results in a managed, in-memory cache so repeated queries return with lower latency instead of re-invoking their data sources every time.
aws_app_sync_api_key: `aws_app_sync_api_key` issues a key-based credential for authorizing requests against an `aws_app_sync_api`, one of several supported authorization modes alongside IAM, Cognito, OpenID Connect, and Lambda authorizers.
aws_app_sync_channel_namespace: `aws_app_sync_channel_namespace` defines a namespace for AWS AppSync Events, the WebSocket-powered real-time PubSub API AppSync supports separately from GraphQL subscriptions, scoping which channels a client can publish to and subscribe against.
aws_app_sync_data_source: `aws_app_sync_data_source` connects an `aws_app_sync_api` to a real backend, a DynamoDB table, a Lambda function, an HTTP endpoint, or another source, that an `aws_app_sync_resolver` then reads from or writes to when a matching query or mutation runs.
aws_app_sync_domain_name: `aws_app_sync_domain_name` registers a custom domain for an `aws_app_sync_api`, so a GraphQL endpoint is reachable at an organization's own domain rather than only at its default AppSync-issued URL.
aws_app_sync_domain_name_api_association: `aws_app_sync_domain_name_api_association` is the actual link between an `aws_app_sync_domain_name` and the `aws_app_sync_api` it should route to. A registered domain with no association routes nowhere.
aws_app_sync_graph_qlapi: `aws_app_sync_graph_qlapi` is the CloudFormation resource type for the same underlying concept as `aws_app_sync_api`, an AppSync GraphQL API, present as a distinct, older resource type in the CFN registry rather than a functionally different resource.
aws_app_sync_graph_qlschema: `aws_app_sync_graph_qlschema` is the GraphQL schema document attached to an `aws_app_sync_graph_qlapi`, the real type definitions AppSync validates queries and mutations against and routes to resolvers.
aws_app_sync_resolver: `aws_app_sync_resolver` maps one GraphQL field to a real operation against an `aws_app_sync_data_source`, written in JavaScript/TypeScript or Velocity Template Language, the actual logic that turns a GraphQL query into a request against a real backend and shapes its response back into the schema.
aws_app_sync_source_api_association: `aws_app_sync_source_api_association` links a source `aws_app_sync_api` into a merged API, AppSync's federation feature for combining multiple independently-owned GraphQL APIs into one endpoint that a client queries as if it were a single schema.
aws_app_test_test_case: `aws_app_test_test_case` defines the smallest real unit of a mainframe modernization test in AWS Mainframe Modernization Application Testing, typically one independent piece of business logic that modifies data, captured against the real mainframe and later replayed and compared against a modernized target.
aws_ecr_repository:
`aws_ecr_repository` creates a real, private ECR repository for storing
container images, with real, configurable scanning and mutability
settings.
aws_iam_policy:
`aws_iam_policy` creates a standalone, reusable IAM policy, a real JSON
document describing what's allowed. It grants nothing on its own,
attach it to a role or user with `aws_iam_role_policy_attachment` to
actually apply it.
aws_iam_role:
An IAM role grants a set of permissions to whatever's allowed to assume
it, an EC2 instance, a Lambda function, another AWS account. `aws_iam_role`
creates the role and its trust policy, real permissions are attached
separately, via `aws_iam_role_policy_attachment`.
aws_iam_role_policy_attachment:
`aws_iam_role_policy_attachment` is the actual grant, it attaches an
existing, standalone policy to an existing role. Neither the role nor
the policy alone grants anything, this attachment is what connects
them.
aws_s3_bucket:
`aws_s3_bucket` creates the bucket itself. Versioning, encryption,
public-access blocking, and lifecycle rules are each their own separate
resource, attached to this bucket by reference, real Terraform provider
behavior since v4.
aws_sqs_queue:
Amazon SQS is a fully managed message queue. `aws_sqs_queue` creates
and configures one, standard or FIFO, with a real, typed binding in
every SDK language.
aws_vpc:
`aws_vpc` creates a real, isolated virtual network, the real
foundation every other real networked resource, subnets, security
groups, route tables, gets placed inside.
